1rm0jji: In Granada, Nicaragua, the streets of the center are full of clothing, hat, and craft shops. To shop you need to point things out (_esta camisa_, _aquel sombrero_), understand prices in córdobas, and ask for what you want politely.
17q3rlg: Este, ese, aquel: pointing according to distance
lywjca: Demonstratives point to a thing and say **how far away** it is. **Este** = near me (here). **Ese** = near you or at a medium distance (there). **Aquel** = far from both of us (over there).
yu90l4: They agree in gender and number with the noun, like an adjective, but they go **before** it: _est**a** camisa_, _es**os** pantalones_, _aquell**as** sandalias_. Notice that the masculine singular is irregular: **este**, **ese**, **aquel** (not _esto_, _eso_, _aquello_).
1avabto: If the noun is already clear, you can use the demonstrative alone: _—¿Qué camisa te gusta? —**Esta**._ Today it is written without an accent mark.
1dcduzu: Variation: in Latin America, in everyday conversation, many people also use **ese** for faraway things, and **aquel** is heard less. In Spain all three distances are used a lot. Both options are correct.
1ffujcr: To remember: each demonstrative has its adverb of place. **este** → _aquí_, **ese** → _ahí_, **aquel** → _allí_. _Aquel_ and _allí_ are the longest words, like the distance.
1fyl3ae: With a masculine noun you use **este**; _esto_ never goes with a noun.
6g4vl5: Esto, eso, aquello: when you don't know the name
ifw8rv: **Esto**, **eso**, and **aquello** are neuter forms: they have no feminine or plural and **never** go with a noun.
ht22b3: They are used for things whose name you don't know (_¿Qué es **esto**?_), for a group of things (_¿Cuánto cuesta todo **esto**?_), and for ideas or situations (_**Eso** es muy caro_; _¡**Eso** es!_).
109pkf1: Compare: _¿Qué es **esto**?_ (I don't know what it is) and _¿Cuánto cuesta **este**?_ (I already know it's a hat and I'm pointing at it).
14ivwdn: If you don't know what the thing is, you don't know its gender: use the neuter **esto**.
1d8rpfp: Numbers from one hundred: prices and quantities
1xrghye: **Cien** is exactly 100: _cien córdobas_, _cien mil_. From 101 you say **ciento**: _ciento uno_, _ciento cincuenta_, _ciento noventa y nueve_. Never _ciento y…_: the **y** only goes between the tens and the ones (_treinta **y** cinco_).
1g7wgjm: The hundreds from 200 to 900 **agree** with the noun: _doscient**os** córdobas_, _doscient**as** camisas_. Three are irregular: **quinientos** (500), **setecientos** (700), and **novecientos** (900).
1otdolo: **Mil** doesn't change: _mil_, _dos mil_, _diez mil_ (never _dos miles_). **Un millón** does have a plural and takes **de** before a noun: _dos millones de personas_.
1ii4nc3: To read a price, say the thousands first and then the rest: 1250 = _mil doscientos cincuenta_; 2499 = _dos mil cuatrocientos noventa y nueve_.
1jvn45e: Currencies on this route: in Nicaragua, the **córdoba** (C$); in Honduras, the **lempira**; in El Salvador, the **dollar**. When writing large numbers, each country uses a period, comma, or space to separate thousands; the Royal Academy recommends a space (_12 500_) or nothing in four-digit numbers (_1250_).
tk44xn: There is no _y_ between the hundreds and the tens.
1dvj1p3: The color goes **after** the noun and agrees with it: _una falda roj**a**_, _unos pantalones negr**os**_. Colors ending in **-o** have four forms: rojo, roja, rojos, rojas (also negro, blanco, amarillo).
1chh3zm: Colors ending in **-e** or a consonant have only singular and plural: _una camisa verde_, _unos tenis verdes_; _un suéter azul_, _unas sandalias azules_; _gris → grises_, _marrón → marrones_.
1sddu9y: **Rosa** and **naranja** normally don't change: _unos zapatos rosa_, _una gorra naranja_. For any color you can say _de color_ + color: _una camisa de color naranja_.
1fg9z4g: Clothing names change by country. _Camiseta_ (Spain, Central America) is _playera_ in Mexico and _remera_ in Argentina. _Chaqueta_ is _chamarra_ in Mexico and _campera_ in Argentina. Sports shoes are _tenis_ in Mexico and Central America. And brown is _café_ in much of Latin America.
x7rlj8: For clothes you ask about the **size**: _¿Qué talla usa?_ (Latin America), _¿Qué talla tiene?_ (Spain). Sizes are usually S, M, L or pequeña, mediana, grande.
1wzaejg: _Negro_ ends in -o: it has a feminine, **negra**.
9q0nzf: In the store: asking, trying on, and deciding
3iaggb: To ask the price: **¿Cuánto cuesta** este sombrero? (one thing) / **¿Cuánto cuestan** estos tenis? (several). _Costar_ is a "boot" verb: c**ue**sta. In Central America you also hear **¿Cuánto vale?**
1cszo51: To ask for another option: **¿Tiene esta camisa en azul?** **¿Tiene una talla más grande?** **¿Hay en talla M?**
1mo02y1: To try on clothes you use the reflexive **probarse** (o → ue): _Me pruebo la camisa_; _¿Puedo probarme estos pantalones?_ And you ask: _¿Dónde **están** los probadores?_
1pzrkxa: After trying something on, use **quedar**, which works like _gustar_: **me queda** bien / grande / pequeño (one thing), **me quedan** grandes (several things): _Los pantalones me quedan pequeños_.
1wbj48s: To decide: **Me llevo** esta / este / estos. If you don't want anything: _Gracias, solo estoy mirando_. To pay: **¿Aceptan tarjeta?** or _Pago en efectivo_. In Nicaraguan markets you can ask for a discount: _¿Me hace un descuento?_
dqey1w: With salespeople you normally use **usted**: _¿Tiene…?_, _¿Me hace…?_ In Nicaragua you will hear **vos** among friends (_¿Vos qué talla usás?_), but in stores _usted_ is the most normal.
ywsdai: The most useful question of the week: **¿Cuánto cuesta este?** + a pointing finger. If you don't understand the number, ask: _¿Puede escribir el precio, por favor?_
yyikfh: For clothes you put on, you use **probarse** (reflexive). _Probar_ without _me_ is for food: _probar la sopa_.
u1yyiw: _Quedar_ agrees with the thing, like _gustar_: _los zapatos_ → **quedan**.

1qfl9hw: The Spanish **d** has two versions. At the beginning of a sentence and after **n** or **l**, it is a **hard d**: the tongue touches the back of the upper teeth and closes off the air. _¡Dos!_, _tienda_, _falda_, _cuando_.
1jhge4v: In other positions, especially **between vowels**, it is a **soft d** [ð]: the tongue approaches the teeth **without closing**, and the air passes. It sounds similar to the English _th_ of _this_, but weaker. _Todo_, _vestido_, _cada_, _verde_, _nada_.
1hz743v: The soft d is very important in shopping: _vestido, todo, ¿cuánto es todo?, pagado, mercado_. If you pronounce it hard like in English, it sounds foreign; if you pronounce it like an English _r_, _todo_ sounds like _toro_.
c1cz9u: Real variation: in the fast speech of Spain and the Caribbean, the d of **-ado** almost disappears: _cansao_ for _cansado_, _el mercao_. And the **final d** (_ciudad, usted, Madrid_) is very weak or not heard at all in many regions. For study, pronounce the soft d, but don't be surprised if you hear it dropped.
afm1jm: The letter is always **d**: the sound changes because of position, not spelling. Don't write _-ao_ for _-ado_: _cansao_ only appears in very informal messages or in texts that imitate speech.
